📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Swiss watchmaker Mondaine has expanded its Doppio collection with the Solar Skeleton, a timepiece that brings solar technology into the foreground of its design.

Rather than concealing the solar plates beneath the dial, the watch reveals them through a precisely cut circular opening, turning a functional component into a defining visual feature.

The design builds on the distinctive visual language of Mondaine‘s Doppio collection, which is characterised by double-line hands and indexes, a concave dial and a double-domed sapphire crystal.

Mondaine explained that these elements establish a sense of repetition, rhythm and structural clarity, while the exposed solar plates introduce an additional layer of depth and visual interest.

While solar technology is typically hidden from view, Mondaine has taken a different approach with the Doppio Solar Skeleton.

A carefully positioned circular opening around the centre of the dial offers a controlled view of the solar movement, while the outer section retains the indexes to ensure clear readability.

By making the technology visible, Mondaine aimed to bridge the watch’s technical function with its aesthetic identity, without compromising the “clarity and legibility” that define the collection.

Powered by a Swiss Ronda solar movement, the watch converts natural and artificial light into electrical energy, which is stored in a rechargeable battery.

According to Mondaine, a few minutes of sunlight can reactivate a fully discharged movement, while a full charge provides a power reserve of up to eight months in complete darkness.

The brand explained that this technology eliminates the need for regular battery replacements, offering a more resource-conscious approach to timekeeping.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton is available in two versions, each offering a different interpretation of its distinctive design.

The first combines a polished silver 316L stainless steel case with a vegan grape leather strap, bringing together traditional watchmaking materials and a contemporary material alternative.

The second features a polished black stainless steel case paired with a matching mesh bracelet, creating a more monochromatic appearance that emphasises the watch’s clean lines and geometric detailing.

Both versions feature a 41-millimetre case, a discreet date window and a precisely laser-etched Mondaine logo and solar markings.

A double-domed sapphire crystal and water resistance of up to 5 ATM complete the design, “combining refined aesthetics with everyday practicality”.

“With the Doppio Solar Skeleton, we wanted to make solar technology part of the design itself,” said Mondaine.

“By revealing the cells beneath the dial, we have created a watch where functionality becomes a defining aesthetic feature, while staying true to Mondaine’s principles of clarity, precision and Swiss design.”.

The Doppio Solar Skeleton reflects Mondaine’s commitment to iconic Swiss minimalist design, where form and function work together.

By integrating visible solar technology into the collection’s established design language, the watch intends to demonstrate how a functional element can become an integral part of a timepiece’s aesthetic identity.

To find out more about Mondaine and the Doppio Solar Skeleton, visit the brand’s website.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.
  • It has been revealed that these machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

It has been revealed that these machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:.

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

According to recent reports, as Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

Sources indicate that “Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe indicates. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”.

Sources indicate that nobbe states WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe claims.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he indicates.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The HEDDphone DX is an open-back headphone that builds on the incredibly popular HEDDphone D1.
  • Sources indicate that why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
  • In the world of audiophile headphones and in-ear monitors (IEMs), second generations of popular products are thick on the ground.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The HEDDphone DX is an open-back headphone that builds on the incredibly popular HEDDphone D1. It has more sub-bass and a more spiky treble, and that's a double-edged sword. Everyone will appreciate its more confident design and its improved comfort, thanks to a new Capra-created headband. But when it comes to tuning, the DX is a softer, warmer take on the lean, mean neutral D1, and I expect that'll enrage as many as it'll delight. For me, the DX is an exciting, musical set that swaps a little detail and imaging for a more fun sound. But at $400 more than the D1, and with a new Capra-created headband released for the D1 early next year, the DX runs the risk of remaining in its older sibling's shadow.

$1,199 is a confusing price point.

Sources indicate that why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

In the world of audiophile headphones and in-ear monitors (IEMs), second generations of popular products are thick on the ground. Last year the divisive Grell OAE was followed with the far better-received Grell OAE 2. Last month the ground-breaking Kiwi Ears KE4 got a second iteration.

Price: $1,199 / £999Release: 24 November 2026Driver & housing: 50mm dynamic driver with thin-ply carbon diaphragm (TPCD); open-backMaterial: Polymer and metal chassis, soft fabric suspension strap, replaceable velour ear padsCable: Detachable dual-sided 3.5 mm ear cup connectors; textile-sleeved cables terminated in 3.5 mm (with screw-on 6.35 mm adapter) and 4.4 mm balancedImpedance: 32 Ω (at 1kHz)Sensitivity: 100dB @ 1mWWeight: 310g.

Sources indicate that so it would be simple to think of the new HEDDphone DX as take two of the best-selling (and my favourite open-back headphone) HEDDphone D1. Simple, but wrong.

HEDD have described it as 'the musical D1', but I think they're playing a risky game. Yes, they took on feedback from their audience, some of whom thought the D1 was a little lean and a touch too clean (not I, for the record). And they also took note of critics of the D1's unforgiving headband (yeah, that thing sucks). But instead of giving us a second take of the D1, I think they've tried to give us the HD 650 to the D1's HD 600. If that was the plan, I don't think they achieved it – but it's a fantastic failure nonetheless.

Big picture: If I were reviewing the HEDDphone DX purely on its tuning, design and comfort, it would be an easy recommendation to all. But the DX costs $400 more than the D1, so it becomes more complicated. To muddy the water further, this January HEDD looks to release the excellent DX headband as a $100 add on for the D1. That will make the D1 far more appealing – and still $300 cheaper than the DX!

So, there's plenty to consider when evaluating the new HEDDphone DX. One thing's for certain: The top spots of my list of the best-sounding wired headphones run the risk of being cluttered with HEDDphones.

Sources indicate that overall, the HEDDphone DX is an exciting, warm open-sounding set, with a very well extended lower frequency, and an immersive midrange. With that lower touch of warmth, it loses much of the crystal clarity of the D1, and some of that higher-end detail. But I still hear a spacious presentation with above-average imaging (the perceived placement of instruments), and enough of what makes the D1 great but with a whopping amount of sub-bass.

HEDD shared a B&K 5128 measurement of the DX with me (above), and it largely replicates what I hear. I definitely hear that slight recession in the 1-2kHz region, and an elevation in 3.5kHz. But for me, the treble's squiggly lines differ ever so slightly (all detailed below). What's clear is that HEDD want the DX to walk the tightrope of warmth and richness, while offering relaxed higher frequencies that give us detail without getting sibilant. And they nail it.

This tuning suits diverse music genres and immersive gaming sessions, delivering clean transient speed, rich tonal body, and fatigue-free playback across dense, complex, layered multi-track studio recordings. I absolutely love it for EDM, but it's not peerless when it comes to vocal tracks, as we will see in the competition section below.

Bass: Most open-back dynamic headphones suffer from sub-bass roll-off, and that's generally been seen as a tradeoff for all that open, expansive presentation of music. The DX holds full sub-bass extension to 20Hz, smack in the middle of the upcoming Headphones.com preference bounds on B&K 5128 measurements.

Warmth between 100Hz and 250Hz reaches the upper edge of that preference band, adding body and fullness to bass guitars and kick drums. According to HEDD's literature, the high-excursion carbon driver moves air with low - basically zero – distortion, meaning we get clean separation in the bass during complex musical passages.

Now, I don't really know how much of that is audible to the human ear. What I do know is that the bass is about as substantial and fun as I can enjoy before things start getting claustrophobic. You see, when bass gets overbearing, lower mids in particular can get swamped by it, and a lot of subtlety is lost. However, what the DX does to combat this is add a treble elevation around 10.5kHz, keeping things from getting too swampy. What you get is a big, detailed, but not bloated bass.

It's a tightrope, but the DX does a fantastic job walking it.

Midrange: With its bombastic bass and sneaky treble (more on that later), the mids of the DX are not really the star of the show. Not at first, at least.

Industry observers note that but there's plenty going on. From 300Hz to 1kHz, the lower midrange sounds correct, not coloured, giving vocals, and string instruments solid weight. Then things get fun. Around 1.5 kHz there's a dip that comes across as relaxed, then a spike around 3.4kHz for me, which is only emphasised more due to the following dip around 5kHz.

All of which is to say, I can really crank the volume with the DX, and the upper midrange doesn't punish me for it. There's no shoutiness, and instead I get fatigue-free listening with coherent vocal articulation that's proportional against the rich low-end. What's more surprising, considering this rollercoaster, is that the timbre of the DX is natural sounding.

For my HEDD DX review I played them through the Luxsin X8 and the Chord Mojo 2 DAC/Amps. These pairings provided ample power delivery and headroom for the headphones, maintaining an uncoloured signal path from source to transducer. Music streamed via Spotify Lossless.

Treble is largely relaxed with the DX, trading sharp brightness for a smooth, fatigue-free approach. I hear reduced energy at 7kHz that lowers sibilance on a brightly mixed track like Sweet Old World by Lucinda Williams. That's not to say there's no bite here, but it never gets in the way of the music.

Industry observers note that though HEDD's B&K 5128 graph reveals a narrow peak at 9-10kHz from their test pinna, for me I got clean treble extension without any glare. Strings, hi-hats, and room ambience retain a crisp texture over longer listening sessions.

I definitely got a bit of spice around 12 kHz, which isn't punishing, but brings with it some micro details, including the mouth clicks of female singers, as with Erykah Badu's Other Side of the Game.

It has been revealed that to call the HEDDphone DX's treble dark is totally wrong. It's balanced, but edges towards modest rather than bright, and I think it'll be enjoyable to a lot of people.

Sources indicate that I think the asking price of the HEDDphone DX is a hard sell. Yours for $1,199/£999, the DX enters a crowded open-back tier, and though I think it does well against many of them, thanks to its excellent German assembly, full part replaceability, and a five-year warranty, I think people will be expecting a truly exotic tuning for that price. That's not what the DX is about.

The HEDD DX matches the planar Audeze LCD-X at $1,199 but at half the weight, measuring 310g. It undercuts the Aune AR9000 ($1,399), HIFIMAN Arya Unveiled ($1,449), Focal Clear MG Pro ($1,490), and Sennheiser HD 800s ($1,999.95), but of course we're talking about a lot of different tunings there.

I think one of its strengths is its chic German design, and its matte black and subtle cream white does a lot to make it stand out from the crowd. The comfort is something many of the heavier contenders could learn from.

I think because the DX is not going for a risky, exotic tuning – which wins over fewer yet more ardent fans – it makes sense to compare it in detail to two mainstream, best-selling alternatives: The HEDD D1 and Sennheiser HD 650.

Sources indicate that for those that missed it, HEDD shook the audiophile world last November with the release of the exquisitely-tuned HEDDphone D1. It was neutral, it was balanced, and for me it didn't seem to have any weaknesses at all. It wasn't warm, but it didn't come across as overly bright. It was about as lean as I can take it before things start sounding cold and clinical. But there was something about its tonal balance where its neutrality came across as rich (though I'd usually use that word to describe warmer sets). It remains my favourite over-ear, open-back headphone to date.

Industry observers note that so, the HEDDphone DX has substantial shoes to fill. But ultimately, comparing them is like pitting Converse against DMs. They're trying to achieve different things... and yet, since they're coming from the same company, and at very different prices, I think the comparison is required.

The D1 is about clarity without exaggerating any part of the mix. The DX is about a good time – whacking up the bass, cranking up that 10.6kHz region to balance it... basically giving you one of the more refined V-shaped sound signatures in a high end pair of headphones.

Sources indicate that of course they share the same DNA when it comes to design and technology. Both headphones share thin-ply carbon drivers, though as said, HEDD positions the DX as "the experience" and the D1 as "the analyst". But that framing understates the musicality of the D1, which remains immersive and engaging despite its neutral focus.

In practice, the DX adds sub-bass weight, upper-bass warmth, a wider soundstage, and a spike up in the treble, whereas the D1 offers tighter bass and overall more focus. Then there's the price. The 'Refreshed' D1, with the latest DX headband and travel case, will sell for $899/£699 in January, while the DX costs $1,199/£999.

Recent findings suggest that for my tastes, and considering the price difference, the D1 remains the one I'd recommend to most people. It has more detail, and due to its neutrality presents music as a massive landscape of sound. The DX is more engaging with its bass and 10kHz shot in the arm, but it's still in its bigger brother's shadow.

However, if you find the D1 too lean, the DX could be what you want.

Both headphones share a warm-leaning, relaxed, largely fatigue-free tuning, but even though it feels neat to make a comparison between the D1 and DX with the HD 600 and HD 650, they're all actually slightly different headphones, with distinct tunings.

The Sennheiser HD 650's sub-bass rolls off from around 90Hz, and even though I think the HD 650's punchy mid-bass is criminally understated by critics, it's still easy to see someone wanting more sub bass than it offers. That's exactly what the HEDD DX does – a sub bass that extends deep to 20Hz.

Recent findings suggest that their midrange presentations are highlights for both headphones, though in subtly different ways. Both offer rich and realistic-sounding vocals and instruments, but I think the HD 650 offers slightly more forward, honeyed vocals, offering more around the 1-2kHz region than the DX, and less around 2.5kHz, giving a sense of space compared to the DX. The timbre of the HD 650 is pretty unbeatable, but the DX gives it a valiant effort.

Sources indicate that the HD 650 is more heavy handed with the upper frequencies, which helps bring texture and grip to the mid-bass that it offers, whereas the DX takes a tamer approach to this region. For me, that makes the DX sound a touch soft, and less striking than the HD 650.

And so, I feel like the DX is actually somewhere in between the HD 600 and 650, rather than neatly comparing directly with the latter.

Industry observers note that though I don't believe it has any impact on the sound profile, it's still worth thinking of the different power needs. The 32ohm DX will run off anything, while the 300ohm HD 650 requires dedicated desktop amplification. Weighing 260g and costing around $500, the HD 650 also remains far more accessible, compared to the still-light 310g but slightly eye-watering $1,199, of the DX. Of course, you have to factor in the far superior build of the DX to the plastic fantastic HD 650.

It has been revealed that if you're not going to miss the sub-bass, I'd still recommend the HD 650 over the DX. It's still my favourite out of the two. But if you know the HD 650 has a little too much spice in the upper frequencies, and you're after a soft, rich midrange – and you're willing to pay over twice the price – the HEDD DX should be on your radar.

Rated at 32ohms with a sensitivity of 100dB at 1mW, the DX is super easy to drive. I had no concerns running it on my Fosi Audio DS2 dongle DAC.

Looking at price point brethren, unlike the 300ohm Sennheiser HD 800 S or the 94dB HIFIMAN Arya Unveiled, it reaches comfortable listening levels from such portable dongles and modest desktop units. A clean solid-state DAC and amplifier with low output impedance gives you excellent driver control, keeping the DX's elevated sub-bass articulate even during dynamic peaks.

Industry observers note that the HEDDphone DX gets 10/10 for build and comfort. It really does excel in these areas, and I feel that this should be the new standard at this price point.

Sources indicate that at 310g, it undercuts most rivals in its price point on weight. A built-in soft, silky suspension strap, designed by the king of headband comfort Capra Audio, is as good as it gets, distributing the weight across your head. We also get updated, super soft velour ear pads.

Clamp force feels firm on initial wear and may bother listeners sensitive to that, though it was fine for me across many hours of music and gaming sessions.

I also love the subtle matte charcoal metal finish, and updated indented metal mesh around the outer-ear. Add to that subtle white patterns on the outer-ear, making the HEDD logo come through, and you've got a very pretty pair of headphones here.

It has been revealed that for $1,199, I'm glad that the DX comes with modular, user-replaceable parts and a five-year warranty. If the tuning is for you, you can expect this headphone to bring you joy for many, many years to come. Excellent work HEDD!

If you've read this review in full, you'll know it's no puff piece – I've made it clear where I think the HEDD DX is lacking. For example, it's less rich and detailed than the cheaper D1. Its above average timbre still doesn't compete with Sennheiser's HD 650, 20 years its senior and a third of its cost. For a sophisticated V-shape tuning, I think its $1,199/£999 price is steep and confusing.

According to recent reports, so why 4.5 stars out of 5? Because the two headphones I've compared to the DX are two of my favourite headphones, and as close to perfect as I've heard.

Taken by itself, I think the DX offers exquisite build and comfort, and sounds fantastic. That half star deduction is because of its price. It's priced so much higher than the (in my opinion) better D1. That's confusing to me. Make them the same price, at least! Make it competitive, HEDD!

If you prefer a little bit more warmth, a far more forceful lower end and less overall clarity up top, then I could imagine that you'd prefer the DX to the D1. But until the HEDDphone DX dips under $1,000, I'm going to find it hard to recommend over the D1.

Beren cut his teeth as Staff Writer on digital art magazine ImagineFX, and has since worked on and edited several creative titles, including Paint & Draw and Computer Arts. As Ecom Editor on Creative Bloq, when he's not reviewing the latest audiophile headphones or evaluating the best designed ergonomic office chairs, he’s testing laptops, TVs and monitors, all so he can find the best tech deals for Creative Bloq’s digital professional audience.

Breaking: Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets.
  • Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant!
  • And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

According to recent reports, farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

It has been revealed that well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Sources indicate that supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Industry observers note that some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:.

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

In a recent development, keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Recent findings suggest that variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

Industry News: "Sacred" archaeological finds become raw materials for design in Ex Situ exhibition

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Latest objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague.
  • Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster, working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin’s profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for new designs: the finds from archaeological digs.
  • However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Latest objects made from mammoth bone, leather from the middle ages and stumps from a road built under Roman Emperor Hadrian feature in the Ex Situ project, set to be exhibited soon in The Hague.

Initiated and curated by Dutch designer Marisa Klaster, working in concert with archaeologist René Isarin, the project makes use of materials that many in Isarin’s profession and the broader public might consider off-limits for new designs: the finds from archaeological digs.

However, while these finds, such as 40,000-year-old mammoth bone and 14th-century ship wood, sound like they belong in a museum, they are in fact deselected – not chosen for inclusion in any archives.

Deselected finds are duplicates, common in type, poorly preserved or otherwise judged to have limited future research value.

Sources indicate that “The material that you see here is the lowest of the lowest quality,” remarked Isarin at a preview of Ex Situ at this year’s Dutch Design Week. “It’s not preserved. It doesn’t belong in a museum. It doesn’t belong in a depot.”.

In fact, if it is not going to be used for educational purposes or reference collections, deselected archaeological finds are required by Dutch law to be carefully destroyed, as they are in many places around the world, stated Isarin and Klaster.

Although the materials may be of low value to archaeology, the designers both found this something of a waste. With Ex Situ, they aim to explore a new category of use and preservation for these materials, believing artists and designers have the capacity to tell stories of heritage in a different way to museums.

With the permission of the province of South Holland, they gave deselected materials to nine Dutch practitioners with expertise in crafts such as ceramics, woodwork and glassmaking.

One of the most finished pieces, exhibited in a preview showcase at October’s Dutch Design Week in the Klokgebouw, was by footwear designer and materials researcher Judith Sanders.

She crafted the foundation posts from a section of the Roman Limes border road, dated to 125AD and built under the emperor Hadrian, into the heel of a pair of high-heeled shoes. Sanders was intrigued by the notion that they could perform structurally once again – this time bearing the load of just one person.

Bold numbers on the sides of the shoe denote where on the dig site the material came from, while a second pair of shoes works leather from the middle ages into a modern-day sneaker silhouette.

Another piece is by designer-maker Daan Simons, who worked with 14th-century wood fragments from a ship that was wrecked and then subsequently used in the construction of Rotterdam.

The texture and existing peg holes in the wood are preserved in his Remembrance Pots, which he imagines holding the ashes of a loved one or a keepsake of theirs, compounding the layers of memory in the vessel.

Klaster and Isarin started on the path to Ex Situ after meeting accidentally at their timber drying kiln, where she was having some wood dried for a furniture project, and he was having the deselected Roman posts dried in the hope they would find another life.

“Intrigued by their blackness”, Klaster asked Isarin if she could have them, and went on to make a series of tall vases. That was five years ago, and they have been discussing the potential intersection of archaeology and design ever since.

Klaster states that the Ex Situ designers were supported with information about heritage and the finds they were working with, but that the project naturally inspired some trepidation.

“In the work that they have made so far, you see that they have thought it through, and there is respect in what they made,” said Klaster. “But the first cut with a scissor or a bandsaw is, of course, a scary thing.”.

Industry observers note that “[One of the designers] was like, can I really saw that in two? And I mentioned yes, you can. If you have a proposal as a designer, yes, it’s yours.”.

That worry will be echoed among some archaeologists, Isarin adds, and he and Klaster’s aim is for the exhibition to promote discussion among the profession.

Sources indicate that “For archaeologists, this material is in a sense sacred,” noted Isarin. “But it’s deselected, so nobody wants it.”.

Sources indicate that he stated that while reactions have so far been positive, the issue becomes more thorny if the design were to take place in a commercial context – for instance, if Sanders’ shoes were sold by a fashion brand. In that sense, some archaeologists may see this project as opening a Pandora’s box.

“As soon as we enter the commercial world, then I think for many archaeologists it will be, even though it’s deselected material, an interesting debate ethically,” stated Isarin.

Recent findings suggest that “Suppose that all this matter, which has no value at all, that somebody gets rich out of it. That would be a disaster for many archaeologists.”.

Nevertheless, Klaster and Isarin think it is a debate worth having.

Pieces in the exhibition come from practitioners ranging from glass artist Bernard Heesen, working with 17th- and 18th-century glass, to conceptual material designer Shahar Livne, working with mammoth bone, and ceramicist Lotte Douwes, working with Roman pottery.

“We have so much rich material beneath our feet, with amazing stories from 40,000 years up to today,” noted Klaster.

The exhibition was previewed at Dutch Design Week, alongside the maximalist installation Everything Moist Seems Alive installation by Maison the Faux and Boris Acket and design collective Show Not Show’s Table of Power exhibition.

Ex Situ: Matter in Translation will be on at See Lab, The Hague, from 5 February to 7 March 2027, with discussion events as part of its programming. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

#115153. Breaking: Arkheron's art director explains why making a beautiful game is sometimes about knowing what to leave out

Breaking: Arkheron's art director explains why making a beautiful game is sometimes about knowing what to leave out

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2299 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Creativebloq

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A lot is going on in Arkheron.
  • In a recent development, built in Unity, Arkheron answers by putting gameplay at the centre of its visual identity.
  • I spoke to Nate Bowden, art director at Bonfire Studios, about Arkheron's world, its characters and the visual language that holds them together.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A lot is going on in Arkheron. Bonfire Studios' competitive multiplayer game drops players into a dark fantasy world where teams battle through an ever-changing Tower, collecting equipment and abilities as they fight. It's fast and chaotic, which creates a challenge for the art direction: how do you make a game look beautiful when players barely have time to take in what's on screen?

In a recent development, built in Unity, Arkheron answers by putting gameplay at the centre of its visual identity. That has shaped the rotating isometric camera, the colourful character designs, and how weapons, animation, and sound communicate information during combat.

I spoke to Nate Bowden, art director at Bonfire Studios, about Arkheron's world, its characters and the visual language that holds them together.

It has been revealed that asked for the first image that made the team feel "this is Arkheron", Bowden doesn't offer one. "I don't know if there was a single piece of art that suddenly made everything click for everyone all at once," he says. "I think Arkheron's visual identity has been something we've discovered and refined over time.".

Recent findings suggest that the look grew up alongside the mechanics. "The IP and its look and feel started in parallel with 'finding the fun' in its gameplay and design," he indicates. "Once the Arkheron that we know and love now started to take shape, art followed suit, and the team started making choices that enhanced the gameplay experience rather than just looked cool for its own sake.".

According to recent reports, if he had to name a single visual idea, it would be the camera. "It would have to be the camera and the choice to make it isometric and also one that rotated around the player," he states. "That helped inform so many decisions on where we should put time and effort.".

It also shaped how the team approached dark fantasy. "I think there's a misconception that dark fantasy has to be relentlessly dark, grim, or oppressive," Bowden claims. One of the team's guiding ideas has been a world that's "hauntingly beautiful", and he thinks they've shown that "you can have environments and characters that have a broad palette of colours and still feel melancholic, mysterious, and dangerous.".

For another game that resists photorealism, read how Blades of Fire flew in the face of modern video game aesthetics, taking a painterly, high-contrast route.

According to recent reports, his example is the rework of Dahla, the game's deadly dancer. The Eternals at the time already resembled today's lineup, but their designs were more detailed, and the palettes were, in his words, "very clamped and constrained". Then came the challenge. "The challenge I put in front of the team was 'we are going to have pink in the game.'".

Industry observers note that "In the end I believe that she turned out not only more vibrant and colourful, but also even more threatening than her original design, which tended to disappear in the shadows," he says. The wider cast now has a broad range of colours, and the payoff is practical. "When you are in those crazy fights, it is so much easier to differentiate the characters from one another from colour alone.".

"Oh man, I could answer this question forever," reflects Bowden when the focus turns to the story behind the Tower.

The short version: the Tower is an afterlife inhabited by Echoes, entities that were once human in the living world. They're trapped in an endless cycle by their own unfinished business, as the Tower builds itself up and then essentially resets. Everything in Arkheron, from someone's appearance to a piece of furniture, is formed from someone's memory, and none of it needs to be accurate. "They're imperfect recollections, shaped by emotion, experience; all rooted in that unfinished business," he says.

According to recent reports, A type of Echo called Builders creates the levels. "Their memories and unfinished business are so strong and profound that they have, in a way, contaminated the tower architecturally.".

In a recent development, "We want the world to feel like it has a history, even when you don't fully understand that history when you begin," Bowden says. Their stories will be revealed as people play, "which is something we can't wait to share.".

Sources indicate that building maps that work as both fantasy spaces and competitive arenas can be difficult, but Bowden is direct in how the art team approached it. "One of the principles I feel most strongly about is that gameplay has to come first. We can create the most beautiful environment imaginable, but if it makes the game harder to understand or less enjoyable to play, we haven't done our job as developers.".

Recent findings suggest that the camera can orbit the action, and players are often fighting several opponents, so they need to read their surroundings almost instantly. That means thinking about silhouettes, landmarks, navigable space and how much visual information players are being asked to process. Bowden doesn't see those as limits. "Quite the opposite; they force us to make stronger decisions.".

In a recent development, where Arkheron's character work puts its emphasis surprised me. "A lot more emphasis is ultimately put on the items vs. the character's bodies themselves," Bowden claims. "That's not to say that we don't put a lot of love and attention there too, but as a player it's more notable that you quickly recognise what that enemy player has equipped, because that's 100% going to impact how you respond in combat.".

So the items get every tool the team has. "Yes, of course we think about colour and shape, but we really live and die by the emphasis we put on bespoke audio, animation, and VFX." He gives three examples:.

"I can literally hear you from offscreen and know when you have switched to Ravah's Crossbow. When you attack with Dahla's weapons, you move like a dancer because you are embodying her with her items. When you use Karriv's abilities, you are literally setting the playspace on fire.".

Industry observers note that the characters themselves have to work at two scales. Up close, they should be "beautiful, detailed, and full of personality". In play, they're seen from an elevated camera, surrounded by other players, abilities and effects. "At that distance, a lot of traditional character detail simply disappears. What remains is silhouette, proportion, movement, sound, and colour," he says. Because players can combine equipment and abilities in different ways, "we're not just designing a fixed cast of characters. We're creating a visual language that helps players understand what they're encountering.".

In a recent development, when thinking about the creative process, Bowden uses the Eternals as an example, whose items are driven by gameplay. Latest ones usually start from a fun gameplay prototype. Sometimes the trigger is a narrative need, and sometimes it's a drawing from the skin design process that "we all just agree needs to be flushed out and developed as an Eternal.".

A small group works out what's missing. If the starting point is a combat prototype, that means working out who the person was in the living world, what their unfinished business was, and what they looked like while alive. Then a larger strike team, with someone from each discipline, hears the pitch of the backstory and abilities. The team gives them "as few visuals as possible", usually just a living-world drawing, and lets them decide how the character will look, sound and move. "That kickoff pitch and backstory is the North Star that we keep referring back to throughout the process.".

In a recent development, "I think the best cosmetics do more than simply make a character look different," Bowden says. "They give players another way to express themselves, and ideally they reveal something interesting about the world." Every cosmetic reflects something about who that person was in the living world, an area of the Tower, or "an ecology or culture that has developed over aeons in this afterlife.".

The team also decided early that although cosmetics are often designed as cohesive sets, players can mix and match between them. "Arkheron is ultimately about cool combinations of items and cosmetics are no exception," he claims. "We've already got some awesome and unanticipated cosmetic combos that our team has put together during our playtests.".

Industry observers note that identity, memory and transformation are already central to the world, which he notes makes exploring different looks for a character feel natural. "I'll give a funny example just to illustrate that," he says. Someone in the living world may have been a baker, and the team could design a baker-themed Echo. But in the lore, that baker may have spent a thousand years in the Tower, mostly in one of the Builders' areas, say the Archivist's level. "That same Echo may now totally take on the look of the level they inhabit vs. what they do or don't remember from the living world.".

According to recent reports, readability sets the limits. "A cosmetic should never leave another player confused about what they're fighting or what's happening on screen," Bowden states. He describes an emote for the Armored Swan skin where you pop angelic wings. "I would have loved to have you fly or float in the air when you use it, but that would be terrible for gameplay and add a lot of player confusion." Size is off the table too, as he says, "I can't have a character skin that is two times larger than the other skins because our hitboxes need to stay consistent for combat and we wouldn't want a player confused for an enemy NPC.".

Recent findings suggest that "One of the most important things we keep beating the drum on is that visual quality isn't necessarily about putting more things on screen," Bowden states. "Often, it's about knowing what to leave out. I like to think of polish as an act of conscious removal.".

According to recent reports, combat is crowded, and there's a natural temptation to make every character, ability, effect and environment as spectacular as possible. "I think that's a trap that happens when you look at any one of those facets in a vacuum," he says. What guards against it is that the whole team plays every day. "My favourite thing about the culture of the whole Arkheron team is that we all play the game every day. That forces all of us to look at everything in context and as a whole and not as one detail over on your own desktop.".

In a recent development, that leads to a set of questions he keeps asking. "What should the player notice first? What's crucial to gameplay? What can remain atmospheric or understated?" Lighting gives environments mood and personality, but it also has to support character and combat readability. Visual effects should make abilities feel powerful and satisfying while letting players understand what's happening and respond.

Recent findings suggest that on PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, the goal is simple. "One of our goals has been to make Arkheron feel like Arkheron regardless of where you're playing it." The game was built from the start to feel great on controller as well as mouse and keyboard, which affects performance, readability, responsiveness, and how much information players see.

Platforms have different technical constraints, so the team has to decide where to spend its resources. "I think there's an crucial difference between preserving every individual visual detail and preserving the artistic intent," he says. The team wants to deliver the atmosphere, character identities, combat clarity, and overall feeling of the world consistently. "And frankly, being disciplined about performance and readability often makes the game better for everyone, regardless of platform. Speaking for myself, the aspect that excites me the most is being able to play with my friends regardless of our hardware of choice.".

Sources indicate that "I hope their first reaction is curiosity," Bowden claims. A video, and especially a screenshot, is likely to give the wrong impression of how the game plays. "You might see that isometric camera and think it's a point-and-click game, or you may see that it is PVP and think it's going to play like a MOBA. It won't." The art, the lore and the gameplay, he says, "are familiar ingredients that are combined in a really original way.".

Sources indicate that it's a game where you're constantly learning: discovering equipment, trying ability combinations, figuring out how to cooperate with teammates, and outplaying opponents. "There's something incredibly satisfying about the moment when all of that starts to click." The art's job is to make that journey feel exciting and intuitive, with a world that captures the imagination, characters and abilities that make you feel powerful, and visual feedback that explains why you succeeded or failed.

His hope for the first hour: "If a player finishes their first hour thinking, 'I have no idea how good I could get at this, but I really want to find out,' I think we've accomplished something pretty special.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Is it time to give your hairstyle and scalp a breath of fresh air? Say hello to the undercut hairstyle, a fashion-forward solution that can elevate your look and promote skin health.

By significantly reducing hair volume, undercuts allow for improved air circulation around the scalp. The result? Less trapped heat and moisture — factors that can contribute to fungal infections, scalp acne, dandruff, and dermatitis.

Whether you’re battling irritation or want to give your “do” a latest lease on life, continue reading to learn how undercut hairstyles can be your ally in style and scalp health.

An undercut involves shaving or cutting hair very short on the sides or back of the head while leaving the hair on top longer.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

It has been revealed that it’s a style that offers a stark contrast and is often used to add an edge to an otherwise conventional look. So whether it’s a side undercut, undercut pixie, mullet undercut, or nape undercut, these hairstyles for women, men, and folks of all genders enhance individuality while offering practical benefits like reduced drying time and less hair maintenance.

Choosing an undercut means embracing a hairstyle with a “heady” mix of aesthetic and practical benefits. Here’s why an undercut might be the refreshing change you need.

Ready to turn heads? The standout feature of an undercut is undoubtedly its unique appearance. Hidden under the longer layers, it packs a punch of boldness you can flaunt or conceal — whatever fits your vibe. You can control the reveal, whether you’re showcasing that edgy undercut for a night out or keeping it classy for the office.

Industry observers note that got a mane that’s more lioness than laid-back? An undercut might be your upcoming BFF. Strategically shaving or trimming the hair short on the sides or back dramatically dials down the volume. This means your thick, voluminous hair becomes way easier to manage and style, turning a heavy head of hair into something light and breezy.

In a recent development, and the best part? You get to keep all the styling potential without any of the hassle. It’s a practical solution that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort.

Are you chasing the clock every morning? An undercut could slash your prep time. With less hair to fuss over, you can breeze through your washing, drying, and styling routine faster than you can say “snooze button.”.

This trimmed-down approach is a time-saver and reduces the daily wear and tear from blow dryers and straighteners, keeping hair healthier in the long run.

In a recent development, undercuts reduce your scalp’s weight and improve hair follicle airflow. This keeps the scalp cooler and reduces the buildup of sweat and oil that can lead to scalp irritation, dermatitis, and dandruff. As a result, undercuts could lead to more robust, healthier hair growth.

Recent findings suggest that ready to shake up your style with a cool undercut? Here’s a rundown of some options to add a dash of daring to your daily look:.

Industry observers note that are you looking for a dramatic change without total commitment? Try the side-swept undercut.

This style features a sleek shave on one side of the head, just above the ear, while keeping the hair on top and the other side longer.

It’s perfect for folks who love to play with contrast — sweep the top hair over to the shaved side for an instant bold statement.

Industry observers note that if subtlety is more your speed, this undercut is a wicked choice. It’s a shaved area tucked away at the back of the head or underneath the top layer of hair so that it can play a fantastic game of hide-and-seek.

Wear your hair down for a business-as-usual look, or tie it up to reveal a sneaky, stylish surprise. It’s an excellent choice for peeps wanting a touch of edge.

Are you feeling bold and artistic? Design Undercuts take personal expression to the next level. These chic undercuts are masterpieces, boasting intricate geometric patterns, sweet floral motifs, or any design that speaks to you.

According to recent reports, do you prefer a more understated yet stylish look? The tapered undercut starts very short near the ear and gracefully lengthens as it ascends the head, blending with your other locks.

It’s a softer version of the undercut that pairs beautifully with bob or lob cuts and offers a gentle nod to the undercut trend without going full-throttle.

The undercut hair offers both style and substance. It reduces styling time and promotes scalp health. By alleviating the weight and allowing the scalp to breathe, undercuts can help minimize challenges like overheating and irritation, especially during warmer months.

It has been revealed that whether you’re drawn to the edgy designs or the subtle tapered style, an undercut could be a clever hack to simplify your morning routine. More time for coffee, less time with the comb!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck.
  • In a recent development, from a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

In a recent development, from a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Industry observers note that finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

It has been revealed that during this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

According to recent reports, need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

Sources indicate that after using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Recent findings suggest that caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Sources indicate that not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

Industry observers note that while generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any concerns.

According to recent reports, hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Sources indicate that remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Images courtesy of Sturdy.

A nine-metre-tall replica of a town hall in Fayetteville, North Carolina, takes centre stage at American rapper J Cole’s world tour set, which has been created by production company Sturdy.

The set for The Fall Off Tour was designed by Los Angeles-based Sturdy to realise J Cole’s ambition to take his hometown, Fayetteville – or “the ville”– “to the world”.

To do this, the studio drew on the historic, two-storey Market House building, which has stood as a local landmark in the city since 1832. Sturdy created a weathered, ivy-covered replica of the structure, which is neoclassical with gothic revival details.

“The Market House was chosen because it’s an iconic piece of architecture historically as well in the town that J Cole’s from,” Martinez told Dezeen.

“I think a big part of the intention is that he takes home with him wherever he goes; conceptually, the idea was to take ‘the ville’ to the world,” he continued.

“And what better way to do that than something that lives basically at the centre point of the entire city?”.

Other nods to the rapper’s life in Fayetteville include the presence of a Honda Civic car, which Martinez describes as a “supporting actor in the show”.

Positioned in front of the building at centre stage, the car is supported on ties that allow it to be suspended above the stage during specific moments of the performance.

“The car is like a supporting actor in the show that adds a little bit of an authentic take to the performance,” he noted.

It has been revealed that “His fans know the black Civic, and, at least from my perspective, with this being The Fall Off, the car needs to have a place in the story. It’s part of ‘the ville’,” Martinez added.

The set was designed by Sturdy to be easily dismantled, shipped and rebuilt between demonstrates across the US, Europe, South Africa, Australia and New Zealand.

This determined the scale and design of the neoclassical Market House replica, which stretches just over 15 metres and is composed of easy-to-assemble wood and metal components.

The materiality of the structure also allows for J Cole’s performance to extend to the building’s first-floor terrace.

Alongside the structure is a 23-metre-long walkway lined with grass, rocks and a tree stump that doubles as a seat for the artist.

“Any show that we are doing, especially of this scale, has to be designed from a ‘rigging perspective’ to how this thing breaks down,” Martinez explained.

“That all has to be thoroughly thought out because we’ve got to be able to have the proper Legos. We can’t really just show up and hope that it’s going to piece together,” he added.

Also contributing to the set is a large LED screen, which, according to Martinez, is used “rather sparingly” throughout the performances to bring the stage design to the fore.

“I think for a long stretch of time reveals were just about crazy visuals and putting stuff on screens and just letting people see stuff moving in the background,” he said.

“We never use the entirety of the screen for the whole show,” Martinez continued. “It’s to add a little bit of depth to what we have going on scenically on stage.”.

J Cole’s The Fall-Off World Tour has been running since July, with recent shows at London’s O2 Arena. The tour will end in December in Johannesburg, South Africa.

Other set designs recently featured on Dezeen include Dave’s London show, which Stufish illuminated with a laser-shooting piano.

It took designers 20 years to bring this font back from the dead

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Paris-based foundry Production Type has revived the classic French typeface Vendôme, restoring it to its former glory.
  • Industry observers note that in its early days, Vendôme was one of the best serif fonts – a celebration of France's post-WWII creative boom.
  • Recent findings suggest that vendôme first made its debut back in 1950, drawn by sculptor and set designer François Ganeau, with meticulous art direction from Roger Excoffon.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Paris-based foundry Production Type has revived the classic French typeface Vendôme, restoring it to its former glory. Once tainted by poor handwritten recreations and clunky scans, the font eventually lost its lustre, but with patience and craft, Production Type has revitalised this classic for the better.

Industry observers note that in its early days, Vendôme was one of the best serif fonts – a celebration of France's post-WWII creative boom. Making a playful, contemporary debut, the upcoming Vendôme Nouveau is a love letter to French heritage, with a elegant, modern refinement.

Recent findings suggest that vendôme first made its debut back in 1950, drawn by sculptor and set designer François Ganeau, with meticulous art direction from Roger Excoffon. Defined by its "leaning stems, wavering strokes, plunging Vs, and abruptly sharp serifs," the typeface became an icon of design, featuring on ads, book jackets, record sleeves, and film posters.

According to recent reports, but the legendary font soon began to suffer from its own success, being recreated by sign painters and shopkeepers who wanted a slice of its fame. With the rise of phototypesetting, the font was endlessly copied, and by the 90s, the iconic typeface had countless iterations with varying degrees of quality and style.

Recent findings suggest that refusing to let the icon die, the Production Type team (and type historian PhDs) set about restoring the font to its former glory. A labour of love, the process took over 20 years of meticulous redrawing, using an array of archival paper proofs and filling the gaps of missing weights from scratch.

The font made an unconventional and wonderfully contemporary debut on the NYC subway, where commuters were snapped reading fake typographic self-help books like “How to Raise a Sans Serif in an All-Serif Family”.

Discover more about the project or take a look at the most iconic typefaces ever made.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

Industry observers note that blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The president of the Royal Institute of British Architects, Chris Williamson, has decided to renew his membership with the Architects Registration Board, nearly a year after terminating it.

In a LinkedIn post, Williamson remarked he was rejoining the Architects Registration Board’s (ARB) register because he no longer wanted “to face the prospect of legal action”.

Specifically, he stated he feared the potential “legal proceedings and financial penalties” from referring to himself as an architect, which ARB does not permit if a person is unregistered.

Williamson’s post comes nearly a year after he revealed he was not going to renew his membership to draw attention to what he called the “absurdity of the current regulatory framework”.

This ARB framework presently only regulates the protected title “architect” and the competence of those on its register, meaning it does not oversee the competence of unregistered providers of architectural services.

His withdrawal from ARB last year aligned with the launch of a campaign by the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) calling for a latest regulatory model for UK architects.

Though he has now rejoined the ARB register, Williamson said his position on the need to reform remains unchanged.

“Today, I have decided to rejoin the ARB register,” he posted on LinkedIn on Friday.

According to recent reports, “Over the last year, I have sat in meetings and roundtables with Ministers, MPs and Peers, spoken at party conferences and COP31, and had the pleasure of awarding the Stirling Prize,” he continued. “Throughout, I have felt the fear of legal proceedings and financial penalties all for referring to myself, in these settings, as an architect – something that’s so fundamental to my identity.”.

Williamson, the co-founder of Weston Williamson + Partners, began his two-year term as president on 1 September 2025.

In the LinkedIn post – a shortened version of an open letter shared with RIBA members – he noted he will now continue to “push for a stronger system” for regulation.

The current RIBA campaign calls for three steps to reform architects’ regulation, including repealing the Architects Act – a UK law that sets the framework for the regulation of the title architect, under which ARB is the regulator.

In a recent development, it also proposes newly introduced legislation outlining reserved activities, such as submitting full planning applications, and who can execute them. The final step calls for the introduction of a Built Environment Council to oversee the competence of individuals and companies working in the construction industry.

“I know my decision to return may surprise or disappoint some of you, particularly those who followed my lead,” concluded Williamson.

“I want to stress this is not a step backwards and it does not reflect a change in my views. In fact, the year I’ve spent outside of the Register has only cemented my commitment to reform,” he continued.

“While my title may change, RIBA’s campaign for regulatory reform will not. I will use my experience on both sides to push for a stronger system that protects what we call ourselves – and what we do.”.

Williamson was selected as RIBA president in 2024. Prior to this, he held several roles within the RIBA, including the vice president international from 2017 to 2019.

In 2014, ARB gave Dezeen 14 days to amend an article describing John Pawson as an architect, claiming it was “in the public interest” for Dezeen to use an alternative description, as Pawson is not registered with the board.
