📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by José Hevia.

Spanish studio Raúl Sánchez Architects turned a former washhouse into Casa de las Lavanderas, with a lightwell that is a “modern translation of the old wells” used by local laundry workers.

The home is located on Barcelona’s picturesque Calle Aiguafreda street, historically an area where washerwomen used wells to handwash their clients’ clothes.

Raúl Sánchez Architects, which won interiors project of the year at this year’s Dezeen Awards, turned one of the old laundry houses on the street into the two-storey Casa de las Lavanderas.

The house is now home to a couple and their newborn baby.

The lower level of the 80-square-metre building was partly underground and very dark, leading the studio to look for new solutions to add more light.

“Since the ground floor is semi-basement, the area furthest from Aiguafreda Street was darker, so to bring light into it, I incorporated this lightwell topped with a skylight,” studio founder Rául Sánchez told Dezeen.

The lightwell also functions as a “modern translation of the old wells” that used to provide water for the laundry workers.

Casa de las Lavanderas faces two streets – Calle Aiguafreda and Calle Granollers – and has entrances on both sides, with the Calle Aiguafreda entrance sitting 1.5 metres lower than that on Calle Granollers.

From here, one flight of stairs leads down to the lower level and the Calle Aiguafreda entrance, and another up to the house’s upper level.

The 40-square-metre lower level houses an open-plan living, dining and kitchen area, a bathroom and a small study.

This can be partitioned off from the living space using folding doors made from wood and rice paper, inspired by the clients’ time living in Japan.

In the kitchen, Sánchez mentioned he added a mirror-clad island to “introduce a sense of fragility without disrupting the open feel of the space”.

Sources indicate that the upper level, meanwhile, houses the home’s bedrooms and a bathroom. The two floors are connected by the Klein-blue lightwell, which has oculi on all four sides to help distribute the illumination from its skylight throughout the space.

Sánchez wanted to “bring that picturesque atmosphere of Aiguafreda Street into the house, making it part of its surroundings by reclaiming that well – now translated into a lightwell that also helps regulate the home’s temperature.”.

This was one of many tailor-made solutions to turn the former laundry house into a home.

“There were many challenges, both technical – access to the mezzanine level, the latest staircase, the structural reinforcements – and functional, like fitting the program into just 80 square metres,” Sánchez noted.

His studio also worked with materials that would complement the existing ones, using terracotta tiles on the ground floor to extend the traditional exterior clay paving and adding colored glazed tiles to the washbasins and bathroom walls.

“Ultimately, the goal is always to create a cohesive, overarching project that addresses all these challenges and offers something extra – something almost hard to put into words, but that translates into simply feeling good in the space,” Sánchez concluded.

Rául Sánchez Architects is presently working on the final phase of the project, the design of its orchard and garden, which will begin at the start of 2027.

The studio also recently designed a concrete home with a sunken courtyard in Cala Tamarit.

Architecture team: Nerea Moya, Marta Gámiz, FlaviaStructure consultant: Diagonal EstructurasEngineering consultant: Mares Engyniers.

5 Signs You’re in a One-Sided Friendship, According to Experts

📅 19 Jul 2024 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship.
  • Most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

Most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going. If that balance consistently feels off—not just once or twice, but over the course of weeks or months—it’s hard not to wonder whether something deeper is going on.

You might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation. They call, if at all, only when they’re bored or when it’s convenient. And then there’s the sharper sting of noticing how effortlessly they find time for other people—just not for you (a surprisingly common frustration you can read more about here).

Sources indicate that to be fair, life can get in the way—people get busy, schedules clash, and our friends can’t always be as available as we’d like—but that doesn’t make it any less frustrating or stop you from feeling resentful when you’re waiting days for a simple “How are you?” But how do you know if this is a temporary lapse or a more unhealthy one-sided friendship? Here are the biggest red flags therapists want you to watch out for.

Look through your texts and DMs: Are you always the first to send a message? When’s the last time they suggested hanging out? You can also experiment by not reaching out to see how long it takes for them to initiate contact. If weeks (or months) go by without a word, their silence may indicate who’s really holding this connection together.

“At a minimum, a good friend (even a busy one) will periodically check in out of curiosity and interest,” Tiana Leeds, LMFT, a therapist based in Santa Barbara, California, tells SELF. After all, someone who truly cares about you should want to know what’s going on in your life, which is why if they consistently don’t try to get in touch (or only expect you to do so), they may not be genuinely interested in your world.

Sources indicate that venting to your friends is natural—some would even argue it can strengthen your bond. That stated, being there for each other is supposed to be a two-way street, Hope Kelaher, LCSW, author of Here to Make Friends: How to Make Friends as an Adult, tells SELF.

Sources indicate that if someone unloads their laundry list of problems but doesn’t listen to yours, “they’re likely using you as their on-call therapist,” Kelaher states. This one-directional dynamic could look like a person who constantly complains about their boss but changes the subject whenever you open up about your work-related stress. Or they dominate dinner conversations with their dating disasters, yet they’re “busy,” uninterested, or MIA when you need relationship advice. Over time, investing all your time and energy into people who won’t give back can drain your energy, Leeds says, and leave you feeling neglected by a person who’s supposed to have your back.

Maybe they insist on eating at restaurants near their place, which means you have to travel across town every single time. They only reach out when “better” prepares fall through (“Hey, my dinner got canceled. What are you doing tonight?”), making you feel more like an afterthought than a priority. More subtly, perhaps they’re only interested in brief 15-minute coffee chats that fit their schedule instead of a dedicated dinner or movie night.

“In a healthy relationship there should always be a give-and-take,” Kelaher indicates, meaning both people need to compromise. So it’s disheartening when, again and again, someone you’d do anything for won’t meet you halfway (sometimes literally).

Recent findings suggest that your friend might be a workaholic or chronically forgetful (which, don’t get us wrong, is still frustrating). But that alone doesn’t mean your bond is one-sided.

Instead, “consider the bigger picture and ask yourself, ‘Is their behavior a reflection of not caring about me, or just a difference in availability and communication style?’” Leeds says. As an example, someone who takes five business days to reply to anyone’s messages may not be singling you out. What’s more telling, though, is if that same person who’s “too swamped” to text you regularly posts Instagram stories of brunches, dinners, and post-work meetups with others in their social circle. Or if your usually punctual friend (who’s known for being reliable) is comfortable canceling intends only with you. These inconsistencies, Kelaher says, suggest that they’re perfectly capable of showing up—just not for you.

Let’s say you mentioned how important it would be to have support at your first 5K race. A friend who truly cares might surprise you at the finish line with flowers, or at the very least shoot over a heartfelt “Good luck!” or “Congrats!” In a one-sided friendship, however, this kind of consideration may be missing entirely. They might downplay your achievement (“Sorry I couldn’t make it, but it was such a short race!”) or forget your massive day without a hint of apology.

True friends go the extra mile to celebrate your successes and be there during tough moments. That’s why if someone repeatedly forgets significant events like your birthday, or rarely highlights empathy for your challenges (like a scary medical procedure, a high-stakes presentation), they may not be as invested as they should be.

Therapists recommended bringing up your concerns non-confrontationally.

In a recent development, ideally, their response can give you a glimpse into whether they’re aware of this imbalance and, more importantly, if they’re willing to work on it. That mentioned, you can’t force someone to be a good friend, so if they don’t care enough to show up for you, know that you deserve better. “After all, friendships take work, Leeds says. “But it’s not meant to be done by just one person.”.

London Museum brings "back a bit of London's heritage" with Smithfield Market opening

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architecture studios Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have completed their long-awaited transformation of the 1880s Smithfield General Market into the London Museum.
  • Opening to the public on Saturday, the former Victorian market hall now functions as a museum that tells the story of London’s history through exhibitions designed by German studio Atelier Brückner.
  • According to the London Museum, it is the largest dedicated city museum in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography by Hufton + Crow.

Architecture studios Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have completed their long-awaited transformation of the 1880s Smithfield General Market into the London Museum.

Opening to the public on Saturday, the former Victorian market hall now functions as a museum that tells the story of London’s history through exhibitions designed by German studio Atelier Brückner.

According to the London Museum, it is the largest dedicated city museum in the world.

Ten years in the making, the opening of Smithfield General Market marks the first phase of the London Museum’s relocation from the Barbican Estate’s former Museum of London, which is set to be demolished.

Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects have overhauled the General Market, which fell into disrepair after it closed in the 1990s, and will also convert the adjacent 1960s Poultry Market, which is expected to open in 2028.

“There’s an opportunity to represent London as it is now and in the future, and really take city museums to another level,” remarked London Museum’s New Museum Project director Alec Shaw.

“We’re bringing back a bit of London’s heritage – one building that has not been seen or encountered for at least 30 years, and the other one an amazing architectural gem that hasn’t been fully appreciated and will now be,” he told Dezeen.

The main entrance to the London Museum is marked by a covered street, West Poultry Avenue, which doubles as the Real Time gallery that stretches between the General Market and Poultry Market.

Entering the transformed Victorian market, visitors pass a museum shop and an auditorium before entering Our Time – an expansive gallery illuminated from above by an oculus.

Shops that once wrapped the perimeter of the market trading floor were removed to open up the space, but the restoration was designed to retain hints of the building fabric’s history.

“You can see pockets in the brickwork walls where joists of the first floor and little plaster columns were originally located,” said Julian Harrap Architects partner Lyall Thow.

“There was a second floor, represented by a darkened band where we didn’t overly clean the brickwork, and fireplaces in the upper offices were taken out, restored, and put back where they would have been originally.”.

Stanton Williams, Asif Khan and Julian Harrap Architects overhauled 42 individual shops that formerly encircled the General Market into 12 multi-storey units.

Six units were kept to contain a restaurant, galleries and learning spaces, while the other six were left for the museum to invite partner institutions to occupy.

“What the ‘museum of tomorrow’ will be is not just a single institute, but a coral reef of small institutes that can plug in – Dezeen could have an office here, a leather upholsterer might have a craft workshop here, restaurants and pop-ups…” remarked Khan.

“This living ecosystem, which is reflective of the city, is possible because of this market building we’ve moved into,” he continued.

“What we’ve done is make openings, windows, and cuts through the floor and ceiling, which allow that energy to emanate out of the city and for the city’s energy to emanate inwards,” added Khan. “At the centre of it all is this enormous public space, the General Market ground floor, where anything can happen.”.

A staircase takes visitors down to London’s Roman street level, to the museum’s permanent Past Time exhibition, which displays precious artefacts.

The restored brickwork walls in the subterranean space are interrupted by a six-metre window, revealing passing Thameslink trains.

A series of underground vaults that were discovered during the museum’s construction will open to visitors in spring 2027.

“This museum epitomises the idea of the primordial reflex in us to dig to find various treasures,” remarked Stanton Williams co-founder Paul Williams.

The architects aimed to make the qualities of the existing spaces work to the museum’s advantage, displaying delicate objects in the underground gallery and maintaining the communal feel of the market space on ground level.

“Decisions based on the building – like precious objects should be kept underground because it’s got a greater thermal inertia – loosen the straitjacket around the museum having to act like a museum in other spaces,” noted Khan.

“It means some other spaces can be more market-like and have a more public-facing potential that a normal museum wouldn’t be able to do,” he continued. “The building has enabled the museum to become a different kind of museum.”.

Unisex toilets were designed in a Victorian style, with decorative tiles depicting wildflowers that grew in London’s bombed-out sites.

Elsewhere in the museum is a 24-hour cafe where original interior tiles and a timber staircase were restored.

Shaw hopes the London Museum will be an inviting place that residents and tourists want to return to time and again.

Industry observers note that “We want to be super welcoming – we don’t want to be intimidating as a museum,” noted Shaw. “Some of the other museums are quite imposing buildings.”.

“We want to be a destination, not just a museum, but a place for people to keep coming back to.”.

Other museums recently completed in London include V&A East by O’Donnell + Tuomey and the V&A East Storehouse by Diller Scofidio + Renfro, which was given a Dezeen Award for its wayfinding design.

Photography by Hufton + Crow.

Like on your face, the pores inside your nose can become clogged with oil, dirt, and bacteria, leading to pimples. These can be painful and may swell, especially in such a sensitive area.

Non-cancerous growths can develop in the nasal passages or sinus lining due to chronic inflammation, allergies, or infections. While they’re usually painless, larger polyps can cause blockages, leading to breathing difficulties, a reduced sense of smell, or recurrent sinus infections.

Recent findings suggest that when you pluck or trim nose hairs, the hair can sometimes grow back into the skin instead of out, causing an ingrown hair. If this becomes infected, it can result in a painful bump inside the nose.

It has been revealed that A bump can also form inside the nose due to trauma, such as a blow to the nose, or even from something as simple as aggressive nose-picking. The trauma can cause the tissue to swell or become bruised. In some cases, a hard bump may form as the tissue heals.

Fluid-filled sacs that can form in your nose, usually harmless but sometimes uncomfortable.

A hard bump inside the nose might be due to problems with the cartilage, such as a deviated septum or cartilage overgrowth.

Small, benign bumps that may appear on or in the nose are often mistaken for pimples but are fibrous tissue growths.

Tech Report: Yes, Your Feet Age. Dermal Fillers Can Help

📅 13 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (999 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that barefoot walks on the beach.
  • Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not fresh, though it is gaining in popularity.
  • It has been revealed that over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that barefoot walks on the beach. A day in their favorite high heels. A long training walk ahead of the Camano de Santiago. These are the goals—big and small—of women undergoing foot filler treatments.

Using an injectable filler—such as hyaluronic acid or body fat—to add padding to sore feet is not fresh, though it is gaining in popularity. As early as the 1960s, medical-grade silicone has been used to puff up padding deflated by age, years of wear and tear, and fashionable footwear, especially high heels. All of this puts intense pressure on the balls of the feet—otherwise known as the metatarsals.

It has been revealed that over time, the fatty cushion on the bottom of your feet dissipates. Fat pad atrophy affects 30% of people over the age of 60. Without that natural cushion, the bones in your feet come into closer contact with the ground, which causes a deep bruise-like pain in the heels or balls of the feet when walking barefoot or standing for long periods.

Industry observers note that for some perspective, look at the doughy wonders that are baby feet and compare them to yours. As we age, wear and tear breaks down that plush tissue. And if you put your feet to heavy use, you’ll wear down that cushion quicker. Some of that internal cushioning can be restored—even if just temporarily—with the injection of dermal fillers.

In a recent development, “It’s getting very popular because people are already familiar with it for aesthetic [uses],” indicates Ben Pearl, DPM, a podiatrist at Arlington Foot and Ankle in Arlington, Virginia. Dr. Pearl specializes in sports medicine and treats endurance athletes looking to restore cushion lost in their feet from pounding the pavement.

According to recent reports, patients don’t have just one choice for injectables, though. Many of the same options available for cosmetic use have also shown promise for feet. There’s hyaluronic acid filler, which adds physical volume and cushioning, and calcium hydroxylapatite, such as Radiesse, which adds firm volume while also promoting fresh collagen growth. Sometimes human body fat is used as the injectable, known as adipose tissue, a practice that is quickly becoming the preferred method.

“[A fat injection] actually recruits your body to rebuild the fat pad in that area so it has a much longer duration,” says Anne Sharkey, DPM, of Soley Podiatry in Austin. Fat allografts from brands like Liposana and Leneva may last as long as two years, compared to hyaluronic acid fillers, which typically need a touch up in six to nine months.

It has been revealed that this type of regenerative medicine is appealing to patients. It’s not a promise that the foot will return to its former glory, but that it will be “as close to normal as possible,” states Dr. Pearl.

Sources indicate that dr. Sharkey and Dr. Pearl have both seen positive results from their patients. Scientific studies corroborate the efficacy of the treatment as well. One small study looking at patients with metatarsal pain found five patients had no more pain six months post-hyaluronic acid injections, and those who still had pain could wear high heels twice as long as they could before the injections. Another study surveying patients who had been injected with body fat reported that their pain improved by more than 70 percent on average, 20 months post injection.

It has been revealed that while there are a growing number of cosmetic clinics offering the procedure, Dr. Pearl cautions against allowing just any injector at it. That’s because injecting filler into feet is a more complex procedure than an aesthetic injection. For one, knowing where to inject requires an understanding of the foot’s pressure points. In his own practice, Dr. Pearl uses ultrasound to help determine where to replace the fat to offload the pain. Additionally, Dr. Pearl notes, the skin is much tougher on the feet than the face, making it a more complicated area to inject.

This is one reason why Dr. Sharkey set up her practice to include a nail salon—combining cosmetology and podiatry. Her patients are already familiar with dermal fillers. Within the attached nail salon you can get manicures, pedicures, ingrown nail treatment, toenail reconstruction, or dermal fillers for feet.

It has been revealed that try not to groan, but it depends. The cost of the procedure is influenced by how much filler is injected, and which brand is used. Other factors that affect cost include how your provider bills the procedure, and how much experience they have with dermal filler injections.

For cosmetic use, the American Society of Plastic Surgeons places the average cost of hyaluronic acid filler treatment at $715. They estimate nonhyaluronic acid fillers, including Radiesse, Sculptra, and Liposana to cost $901 on average per treatment. However, the feet will almost certainly require more filler than the face, so you can expect the cost to be higher.

It has been revealed that but will insurance cover it? Unlikely. “Even though it isn't technically cosmetic, it may not be considered medically necessary, because these procedures are often considered elective and cosmetic branding has a box drawn around it,” states Mark Welter, chief strategy and growth officer at Welter Healthcare Partners, a healthcare business management firm.

If you’re transparent with your provider about any financial concerns you have, they can work with you to find a middle ground between pain relief and high costs. Dr. Sharkey, for example, will often offer her patients more affordable hyaluronic acid fillers as temporary pain relief until they’re ready to dive into a more expensive fat injection.

It has been revealed that if injectables aren’t accessible to you, there are other ways to deal with foot pain. Here are some options, most of which require a low financial investment.

A podiatrist can help walk you through any of these options and come up with a plan to minimize your pain.

#115092. Tech Report: Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging architect of the year Kuma&Elsa

Tech Report: Five key projects by Dezeen Awards emerging architect of the year Kuma&Elsa

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dezeen

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This year Kuma&Elsa was named emerging architect of the year at the Dezeen Awards.
  • Led by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French-Spanish urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa has completed a wide variety of projects from their bases in France and Japan.
  • “We believe it is vital not to impose a common consistency across our projects,” Kuma told Dezeen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This year Kuma&Elsa was named emerging architect of the year at the Dezeen Awards. Here, they select five projects that demonstrate the ethos of the studio.

Led by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French-Spanish urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa has completed a wide variety of projects from their bases in France and Japan.

“We believe it is vital not to impose a common consistency across our projects,” Kuma told Dezeen.

Recent findings suggest that “Every project is unique, shaped by a one-off combination of site and client. Preserving that uniqueness requires an open mind. Personally, I promptly lose interest when things are planned in advance.”.

“That stated, there are certain topics, many of which are shared by our generation, such as feminism, the care for natural resources and a shared public space, that interest us on a personal level, and I imagine they find their way into our work,” added Escobedo.

“We try to approach them with a sense of joy.”.

Although they have already designed a wide range of projects, from installations to houses and public toilets, the duo would like to work on more varied schemes and unusual projects, along with completing their own, long-running renovation.

“It would be nice to actually finish this self-renovation project at some point…” noted Escobedo.

“More seriously, I’d love to experiment with the reuse of materials on a larger scale, or in a European context, working with European craftspeople.”.

Recent findings suggest that “I would love to work on overlooked building types and uses, especially those that have little place in architectural history and attract few expectations,” added Kuma. “Designing a toilet pavilion for the Expo, a building type that nobody expects to become architecture, is one example.”.

Along with the variety in projects, both architects agreed that the wide range of daily activities is what they most enjoy about being an architect.

“The variety, the diversity,” noted Escobedo, when asked about her favourite part about being an architect.

“One day you’re on a construction site with incredible Japanese carpenters, the next you’re discussing a detail with your favourite thermal engineer, the following week you’re taking part in a conversation with colleagues you admire, before finding yourself struggling to install the plumbing and tiles in a shower because you had the brilliant idea of taking on a self-build project.”.

Kuma also added that he enjoys the intensity of working on site.

“The construction site,” he noted. “Nothing is more stressful or demanding, with all the struggles involving people and money. Yet every time I see a building taking shape, I feel glad I chose architecture. There is something addictive about it.”.

Read on to find out five key projects by Dezeen Award-winning studio Kuma&Elsa, as described by the duo:.

Nakano House, Tokyo, Japan, 2026.

“The client’s childhood home, a traditional Japanese house, has an engawa gallery open to the garden. The upcoming residence occupies the top two floors of a building owned by the client. She, along with her two sons and their families, will move into three apartments located on the sixth and seventh floors.

Recent findings suggest that “At the centre of each apartment, we inserted a hut-like volume that gathers the quieter rooms: a small living room and the bedrooms. In the space carved out around it emerges an intermediate zone – an engawa that serves both as a place to stay and as a passage.

“Balcony, engawa, and hut thus form three spatial layers that resonate with the childhood home. The structure consists of Y-shaped modules made of lightweight steel sections and bracing cables, typically used in shelving systems.

Sources indicate that “These modules are arranged two by two in mirrored pairs along a regular grid, with occasional inversions. From these newly introduced dwellings, one can look down across the street at the engawa of the childhood home. This project does not seek to nostalgically replicate that memory-laden place, but rather to build a new home nourished by the memories of the old one.”.

According to recent reports, “One water is a bathing and rest pavilion for the Osaka World Expo 2025. Toilets are at first glance a pragmatic facility, dedicated to human physiology. But they are also intimately linked to contemporary challenges such as the use of natural resources and gender.

“One water uses the path of rainfall on the accessible roof and its subsequent accumulation to create encounters between water and the public, and contribute to the supply of the toilets.

“The design of the pavilion allows for the reuse of materials and structural components, and makes no gender distinction in the toilets, because, after all, ‘we are all fish in one water’.”.

House by the temple, Saitama Prefecture, Japan, 2024.

“The house is opposite the entrance of a temple that is surrounded by a park of ancient trees and a wall, as if it belongs to another world. Reflecting this closed composition, we designed the house as an everyday world for a family.

Industry observers note that “The main building is located at the back of the plot and has a quarter-circle initiative to reduce its own shadow. The street facade is a single-storey hut, which creates a continuity between the open space of the park and the garden of the house.

In a recent development, “On the ground floor, the park is the backdrop to the house. On the first floor, each room offers distant views of the temple, like an observatory.”.

Yamada House, Fukuoka, Japan, 2020.

In a recent development, “A daily public space in a residential area. We create a plaza in a small residential area where human life is still at human scale.

It has been revealed that “The house is like the background that forms the square. The composition consists of various couples: the smooth black mortar of the outer wall and the rough crushed black basalt ground, the emerald entrance hut and the crape myrtle tree with white flowers, the interior spaces and the outside square.”.

Water Flower Courtyard, Montpellier, France, 2019.

In a recent development, “The life of a flower is short: we wanted to express the fragility of a concentrated life from flowering to dispersal. This project was open to the public for a week during the Montpellier architecture festival Festival des Architectures Vives in June 2019.

“Eighteen lightweight units made of two-millimetre-thick aluminium sheets are laid out together as a forest.

Recent findings suggest that “The tube is a vase that contains water and peony flowers, the bowl contains water and slate stones. All structures are self-supporting and their stability works as in a roly-poly toy. After a few days, petals start falling on the surface of the water.”.

The Portuguese Directorate-General for the Arts announced on November 16 the curatorial proposal that will represent the country at the 20th International Architecture Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia in 2027. The selected project was "Mãos ao Chão (Hands on the Ground)," an artistic and curatorial proposal by Joanna Alice Helm, Remígio van Eys Chilaule and Samuel de Brito Gonçalves. It was chosen from a limited competition among three teams. The other two proposals were "Analog Twins" by Alice Clanet-Hallard, Edgar Brito, Francisco Lobo and Romea Mury, and "Matéria Viva — Os materiais da construção portuguesa e o saber que resiste" by Helena Botelho. The evaluation committee was composed of Álvaro Domingues, Andreia Garcia, João Gomes da Silva, Mariana Pestana and Tânia Teixeira.

Sources indicate that "Hands on the Ground" invites Cabo Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique and São Tomé and Príncipe, countries without permanent representation at the Biennale, to the Portuguese Pavilion. The four countries are former Portuguese colonies that now maintain close diplomatic, cultural and economic ties with Portugal. Portugal established trading posts, settlements and colonies across these territories starting in the 15th century and exercised administrative authority over them until their independence in the 1970s. Together with Angola, the four form the PALOP (Países Africanos de Língua Oficial Portuguesa), and all five belong to the Community of Portuguese Language Countries (CPLP).

The invitation draws on a Finnish gesture from 1976, when Finland ceded its space to showcase Portuguese architectural knowledge. Unlike other European countries, Portugal does not have a permanent national pavilion building. Its exhibition will be hosted at Fondaco Marcello, a 15th-century building on the Grand Canal, which also hosted the Portuguese exhibition at the 19th Venice Architecture Biennale in 2025. "Hands on the Ground" proposes to include the African countries as "a source of learning, not a distant object." The curatorial approach organizes content into six overarching themes: extreme climates, local materials, passive responses, memory and innovation, ways of doing, and toward building the future. Local authors are invited to develop critical manifestos on these topics in different formats.

What Is ‘Fiber Training’—And Why Should You Be Doing It?

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1177 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that with the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one problem keeps coming up: the side effects.
  • Industry observers note that to be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet.
  • But if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that with the fibermaxxing fad encouraging people to prioritize this chronically neglected nutrient, one problem keeps coming up: the side effects. As crucial as hitting your daily fiber goal is, your body doesn’t always make doing so easy. Fiber is difficult for your digestive system to break down and has to be handed off to bacteria in the colon instead (which is kind of its point), so piling on too much too fast can result in a barrage of painful, awkward, or inconvenient digestive symptoms—bloating, gas, stomach cramps, the whole nine yards.

Industry observers note that to be clear, GI distress isn’t a sign to abandon your pursuit of a higher-fiber diet. “Even with fiber becoming a growing trend, people still greatly underestimate its importance and, also, just how many ways it benefits the human body,” Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. You’re probably familiar with fiber’s ability to keep you full, stave off constipation, and support gut health, but it wears plenty of other hats too, like lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol and stabilizing your blood sugar (not to mention reducing your risk for a slew of diseases in the long run). In fact, overlooking fiber is one of the top nutrition mistakes people make, according to experts.

But if you feel apprehensive at the thought of fighting constant stomach discomfort in the process of working to correct a fiber deficiency, we don’t blame you. In fact, it’s a complaint that Lisa Ganjhu, DO, a gastroenterologist at NYU Langone Health, hears all the time at work: “I have a lot of patients that will say ‘I ate more fiber, and now I’m really bloated and crampy,’” she says. Thankfully, there’s a way to curtail those disagreeable side effects so you can (comfortably) continue your fiber journey: a strategy Nielsen calls fiber training. Here’s what that involves, and how to start developing those “muscles.”.

According to recent reports, fiber training is exactly what it sounds like: training your body to handle fiber better. It’s all about “slow, consistent increases in fiber to help you build your tolerance…while minimizing the potential symptoms,” Nielsen notes.

You can think of fiber training kind of like preparing for a race. “In much the same way that you wouldn’t go out and run a marathon tomorrow if you haven’t run a mile before,” you need to work your way up to a high-fiber diet, Nielsen notes. Similarly, Dr. Ganjhu compares it to a weightlifting regimen. Rather than lifting 50-pound weights right off the bat, “you kind of have to adjust slowly,” she says. “You start off with 10. When that becomes easy, you go to 20, then you go to 30”—and so on.

Recent findings suggest that fiber training is especially critical if you’re constipated at the outset, as many people are, according to Nielsen. Even though fiber can help prevent and alleviate constipation, too much at once can actually make an existing concern worse by overwhelming your gut. “When you add a ton of fiber to an already backed-up system, it’s kind of like a bottleneck on the highway,” Nielsen indicates: If you try to shoehorn four lanes into one, you’re going to end up with a jam on your hands.

Now that you know fiber training entails steadily increasing your fiber intake, you’re probably wondering what that looks like on a more practical level. Before we share specifics, some context for how much fiber you actually need might be helpful. Per the federal Dietary Guidelines for Americans, 2020-2025, women should aim for 28 grams of fiber daily from ages 19 to 30, 25 grams of fiber daily from ages 31 to 50, and 22 grams of fiber daily starting at age 51, though some experts recommend even more—a helpful set of parameters if you’re not sure where to start.

While the ideal amount of fiber to add to your diet while fiber training can vary from person to person depending on health needs (like a constipation issue), most people are “looking at [adding] probably three to five grams at a time,” Nielsen says.

With that in mind, you’ll want to choose a food that has a fiber content in that ballpark—say, an apple (around four grams of fiber), a half-cup of chickpeas (around five grams of fiber), a tablespoon of chia seeds (around five grams of fiber), or two tablespoons of ground flax (around four grams of fiber)—and eat a serving every single day until you feel like your body has adjusted (read: you’re not experiencing any additional bloating, gas, or other GI side effects). This process typically takes around five to seven days, according to Nielsen, but everyone’s digestive system is different, so don’t worry if you need more (or less!) time. “It really is about listening to your body and individualizing the rate at which you increase,” Nielsen indicates. “You have to follow your symptoms and go slow,” Dr. Ganjhu agrees.

Then, you can tack on another dose—like a second apple, a full cup of chickpeas, two tablespoons of chia seeds, or four tablespoons of ground flax. Continue increasing your fiber intake in these increments (and at this pace) until you’ve hit your daily fiber goal. If you’re a 35-year-old woman starting from scratch, reaching 25 grams of fiber—the recommended daily amount for that age—would take around five five-gram doses, six four-gram doses, or eight three-gram doses, for example.

People who are constipated may want to specifically fiber train with foods that are low in FODMAPs—fermentable carbohydrates particularly hard on sensitive stomachs—according to Nielsen. Like we said above, increasing your fiber intake when you’re backed up can, well, backfire, so low-FODMAP foods are more likely to be a safe bet than their high-FODMAP counterparts. Kiwis, which contain four grams of fiber in a two-fruit serving, are an especially strong option if you fall into this category (and they’ve even been specifically studied as a dietary constipation treatment), Nielsen says. Similarly, she adds, a gentle fiber supplement like Metamucil, which is made from psyllium husk, also “provides a lot of the benefits, but tends to be less irritating to a troubled system.”.

Industry observers note that another tip: If you’re constipated, make sure to drink plenty of water as well (though the oft-referenced eight-glasses-a-day requirement is something of a myth!). Because fiber needs water to work its stool-softening magic, insufficient fluids could leave your bowel movements hard and dry, exacerbating the problem.

In a recent development, whatever latest fiber sources you choose, taking this slow-and-steady approach should help ease the transition to a higher intake. “If you’re someone who doesn’t eat a lot of fiber and all of a sudden you start eating 30 grams of it, the colon is just not going to know how to manage that efficiently,” Dr. Ganjhu says. But by leveling up little by little? You can heighten that “colonic fitness”—and sidestep the worst of the awkward stage.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The 16-foot (4.8-metre) tree, which was unveiled this week, sits in the entrance hall of the Victoria & Albert Museum (VA’s) South Kensington location and was designed to celebrate craft and creativity.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Photography courtesy of Burberry.

Fashion brand Burberry‘s chief creative officer Daniel Lee worked with artist Ann Carrington to create a Christmas tree sculpture for the Victoria & Albert Museum, made from “memories, traditions and little treasures.”.

The 16-foot (4.8-metre) tree, which was unveiled this week, sits in the entrance hall of the Victoria & Albert Museum (VA’s) South Kensington location and was designed to celebrate craft and creativity.

“This collaboration with Ann is a celebration of creativity and what better place to showcase this than the V&A?” Lee mentioned. “It’s one of my favourite museums and a constant source of inspiration to me.”.

Lee and Carrington made the tree from old money boxes, biscuit and sweet-tin lids, trinket dishes, silver trays, horse brasses and embossed plates, which were turned into rosettes and ribbons and attached to a metal frame.

The tree, which was made as part of Burberry‘s 170th anniversary celebrations, also features ribbons and bows made of scrap metal.

Industry observers note that according to Lee, he and Carrington made the sculpture from “memories, traditions and little treasures. Objects and materials that most people would overlook.”.

Carrington added that the design was inspired by the ritual of getting old Christmas decorations out of storage in time for the festive season.

“We wanted to capture that magical moment when you retrieve the battered old box of Christmas decorations from the loft, sift through the faded party bows and tattered tinsel accumulated through the generations and begin the joyful ritual of dressing the tree,” she said.

“I’m always drawn to work that’s handmade, and Ann is a master of her craft,” Lee said of the collaboration.

As well as the tree, the V&A will also be showing The Burberry Trench: Crafting an Icon, a display that traces the history of the trench coat. Burberry has a multi-year partnership with the museum and is set to open The Burberry Gallery at the South Kensington location in 2028.

Lee has previously unveiled an archive-inspired logo for Burberry, and a few years ago, the brand revealed its redesigned London flagship store.

Photography courtesy of Burberry.

Industry observers note that the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) concluded on November 22, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, following negotiations that extended beyond the scheduled closing date. Hosted by Türkiye with Australia leading the negotiations, the summit brought together representatives of nearly 200 Parties, alongside researchers, businesses, climate organizations, and civil society, to advance international climate action. While countries reached decisions on climate finance, adaptation, just transition, and other agenda items, they failed to agree on the proposed overarching Antalya Pact, with disagreements over fossil fuels, finance, and the level of ambition in the final text. For the built environment, COP31 advanced several initiatives addressing building energy performance, electrification, urban resilience, and climate investment, while leaving broader questions of implementation and international coordination unresolved.

For the built environment, COP31 advanced several initiatives addressing building energy performance, electrification, urban resilience, and climate investment, while leaving broader questions of implementation and international coordination unresolved.

According to recent reports, buildings and construction remain central to climate action, accounting for a significant share of global energy consumption and emissions while also being exposed to rising temperatures, flooding, and other climate-related risks. At COP31, the Turkish Presidency introduced the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, a voluntary framework targeting a 25% reduction in the operational energy intensity of the global building stock by 2035, compared with 2020 levels. Discussions on urban resilience also addressed the relationship between national climate commitments and investment at the local level, particularly in housing, infrastructure, and adaptation. While these initiatives provide frameworks for further action, their implementation will depend on national policies, financing, and coordination across public and private sectors.

The Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings.

One of COP31's most direct initiatives for the building sector was the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, debuted by the Turkish Presidency on October 29 in collaboration with the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)-hosted Global Alliance for Buildings and Construction (GlobalABC). The voluntary framework supports two of the Presidency's 2035 objectives: pursuing a 25% reduction in the operational energy intensity of the global building stock compared with 2020 levels, and accelerating efficient electrification in buildings in support of the 35-by-35 target, which seeks to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. At the second ministerial meeting of the Intergovernmental Council for Buildings and Climate (ICBC), held during COP31, 24 countries, the European Commission, and 38 non-Party stakeholders expressed support for or endorsed the Compact.

The voluntary framework supports two of the Presidency's 2035 objectives: pursuing a 25% reduction in the operational energy intensity of the global building stock compared with 2020 levels, and accelerating efficient electrification in buildings in support of the 35-by-35 target, which seeks to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. At the second ministerial meeting of the Intergovernmental Council for Buildings and Climate (ICBC), held during COP31, 24 countries, the European Commission, and 38 non-Party stakeholders expressed support for or endorsed the Compact.

Industry observers note that the framework identifies six areas for action, including integrating energy efficiency and electrification into national strategies, strengthening building energy and carbon performance, accelerating renovation of existing buildings, reducing energy demand, improving buildings' flexibility within energy systems, and mobilizing finance and technical capacity. Its proposed measures range from stronger building energy codes and renovation strategies to electrified heating and cooling, energy management, passive cooling, and investment in public buildings and social infrastructure. While the Compact does not establish binding targets for individual countries, it provides a shared framework for governments and industry to advance building decarbonization, linking operational energy performance with renovation, affordability, and long-term resilience.

Climate-Resilient Cities: Housing, Infrastructure, and Local Implementation.

Cities and urban resilience were also prominent at COP31, with the Turkish Presidency and UN-Habitat convening a High-Level Dialogue on Urban Resilience, Adaptation and Climate Action on November 12. The discussions addressed how national climate plans and adaptation strategies can be translated into investments at the local level, with housing, infrastructure, urban regeneration, informal settlement upgrading, and post-disaster reconstruction identified as areas requiring stronger implementation. Participants emphasized the importance of connecting national climate commitments with local development priorities while strengthening coordination between governments, municipalities, financial institutions, and development partners. The dialogue also highlighted the financing gap facing cities, with climate-resilient infrastructure and services requiring investment beyond current levels.

The discussions positioned housing and basic urban services as part of climate adaptation, highlighting the need for homes that can withstand floods and extreme heat, infrastructure that can continue functioning during climate-related disasters, and urban development strategies that address the needs of vulnerable communities. Rather than treating resilience as a separate technical objective, the discussions linked it to housing conditions, public services, reconstruction processes, and the capacity of cities to respond to climate risks. Financing Urban Resilience Through the Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility.

According to recent reports, alongside discussions on climate adaptation, COP31 highlighted the Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility (SURFF), an initiative developed through Türkiye's İLBANK in partnership with UN-Habitat and the World Bank. Introduced ahead of the summit during Newly introduced York Climate Week, the initiative aims to help cities and countries translate climate commitments into investment-ready urban resilience projects, addressing the gap between national climate strategies and implementation at the municipal level. It is structured around three pillars: country-led Resilient Cities Platforms, a Resilient Cities Centre of Excellence, and an international dialogue intended to facilitate cooperation, share experience, and improve access to climate finance.

SURFF was presented as an approach to strengthening project preparation, local institutional capacity, and access to public and private financing for urban climate investments. Its priorities include resilient infrastructure, climate adaptation, and projects that respond to the needs of cities and their communities. Rather than operating as a upcoming financing fund, the facility aims to connect cities with existing financing mechanisms, technical assistance, and implementation partners. Its effectiveness will therefore depend on the development of investment pipelines, the availability of finance, and the ability to translate its framework into financed and completed urban interventions.

Fossil Fuels and Electrification: An Unresolved Transition.

Recent findings suggest that the transition away from fossil fuels remained one of the most contested concerns at COP31. Countries were divided over whether the final political text should include an explicit commitment to move away from coal, oil, and gas. The proposed Antalya Pact did not include a clear reference to fossil fuels, prompting objections from the European Union, the United Kingdom, and several climate-vulnerable nations, which argued that the text did not adequately address the primary drivers of climate change. Disagreements over the language of the energy transition, climate finance, and the level of ambition required prevented the draft from reaching consensus. The outcome leaves the commitment made at COP28 to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems without a new collective roadmap at COP31.

In a recent development, outside the formal negotiations, efforts to advance electrification continued through voluntary initiatives. Around 80 countries supported the Presidency's 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, which seeks to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. For the built environment, electrification connects the transition to buildings through heating, cooling, cooking, and energy systems, while energy efficiency and passive design strategies can reduce demand. The Antalya Compact similarly addresses building energy use through renovation, efficient systems, and measures to reduce operational demand. However, electrification targets and building efficiency initiatives do not replace a negotiated global commitment to phase out fossil fuels, leaving the pace of transition dependent on national policies, energy infrastructure, investment, and further international cooperation.

Why Are People Taking CoQ10 Supplements for Longevity, and Do They Work?

📅 14 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility.
  • In a recent development, the appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol.
  • Recent findings suggest that that role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Coenzyme Q10, or CoQ10, was once a niche supplement, known best in wellness circles for its possible benefits for heart health and fertility. But now the antioxidant’s star is rising for a upcoming reason: its purported longevity-boosting powers.

In a recent development, the appeal of CoQ10 has grown as researchers have explored its effects on various conditions, with small studies revealing, for example, it may help boost insulin sensitivity, cut the frequency of migraine attacks, and alleviate muscle aches from statins used for high cholesterol. But as of late, there’s excitement around its broader anti-aging potential because of how it supports our mitochondria, which you may remember from high school biology as the “powerhouse of the cell.”.

Recent findings suggest that that role has punched CoQ10’s ticket into the longevity club, alongside other supplements thought to lend a hand to mitochondria (like urolithin A and nicotinamide mononucleotide, or NMN). There’s even a synthetic derivative of CoQ10 designed specifically for better absorption by mitochondria, which is called mitoquinone (or MitoQ), that’s gaining hype among celeb trainers and athletes for boosting energy, recovery, and “cellular health.”.

Sources indicate that but is CoQ10 all it’s cracked up to be when it comes to longevity? Read on to learn more before grabbing a bottle of this supplement.

Industry observers note that our cells naturally produce CoQ10, a molecule that acts like a conveyor belt for charged particles inside our mitochondria, enabling them to “efficiently create adenosine triphosphate, or ATP,” the “currency for cellular energy,” Anthony Molina, PhD, a professor of medicine at UC San Diego who studies aging biomarkers, tells SELF. That’s a major deal, as all cells rely on that energy to complete their daily functions. As we age, both the number and energy-producing powers of mitochondria drop off—a process involved in the development of many age-related diseases, Dr. Molina points out. Meanwhile, CoQ10 levels also decline with age, leading to the idea that we should take it in supplement form for better mitochondrial (and, in turn, overall) health.

Beyond its role in energy production, CoQ10 is also an antioxidant that is “very powerful in capturing free radicals,” or volatile molecules that can harm cells, Daria Mochly-Rosen, PhD, a professor of chemical and systems biology at Stanford University and coauthor of The Life Machines: How Taking Care of Your Mitochondria Can Transform Your Health, tells SELF. By stabilizing those molecules, CoQ10 may help to keep that damage (a.k.a. oxidative stress) from piling up and also contributing to aging and the development of chronic disease.

Recent findings suggest that separately, CoQ10 has potential benefits as it relates to cardiovascular health: It’s anti-inflammatory and may also improve the function of blood vessels, helping regulate blood pressure, JoAnn E. Manson, MD, DrPH, chief of the division of preventive medicine at Brigham and Women’s Hospital and professor of Medicine at Harvard Medical School, tells SELF. These upsides could lower risk for heart disease, the number-one killer in the US.

Despite the promising mechanisms above, “the evidence base just isn’t yet there,” Dr. Manson states. The studies we do have on CoQ10 and longevity are in mice and rats—and while a few suggest a lifespan-extending effect, or a way to reverse some cognitive decline once it starts, others show no anti-aging upsides in healthy animals. Besides, “we find again and again that humans are not just large, non-hairy mice,” Dr. Mochly-Rosen points out, “so we can’t assume the results transfer.”.

Studies in people have been focused on CoQ10 as an intervention for specific diseases, particularly cardiovascular ones. All the experts say the strongest evidence for longevity is in those with heart failure, who have low CoQ10 levels—taking the supplement alongside standard treatment has been shown to reduce the need for hospitalization and risk of early death, possibly because of its mitochondrial perks.

But logistically, it’s a lot trickier to prove that CoQ10 prolongs life in healthy people versus in those with a medical condition or known CoQ10 deficiency. In the absence of these studies, it might be tempting to take a logical leap: If we know CoQ10 supports mitochondrial function, and levels of both dip with age and disease, supplementing with CoQ10 seems like it should help you live longer. But the problem is, we don’t know exactly what drives the mitochondrial concerns that occur with age, Dr. Molina indicates. “So maybe you’re not taking a shot in the dark because we know that mitochondria has something to do with healthy aging, but using CoQ10 as the tool is like taking a shot in a dimly lit room,” he says. “It’s not clear whether you’re hitting the right target.”.

According to recent reports, as with any supplement, it’s best to ask your doctor before adding CoQ10 to your routine. While there’s a good deal of data to suggest it’s safe and well-tolerated, there are some people who shouldn’t take it, generally because of interactions with prescription drugs, Dr. Molina points out. The main concern is with blood thinners (a.k.a. anticoagulants) like warfarin (which are often prescribed after a blood clot)—CoQ10 could make these drugs less effective, Dr. Manson notes. It’s also extra key to check in with your doctor first if you take insulin or are receiving treatment for cancer. Though CoQ10 doesn’t usually cause side effects, you could also wind up with some mild GI upset or insomnia, Dr. Manson adds.

There’s also the quality-control problem that comes with any supplement. These are not subjected to the same FDA regulations as medications are, meaning you can’t know for sure that you’re getting what the bottle promises. Studies of certain CoQ10 supplements have found that they contained less of the antioxidant than the amount listed on the label, Dr. Mochly-Rosen notes. Your best defense against winding up with a sugar pill is to find a product that’s been third-party verified, she indicates—look for the “NSF certified” or “USP verified” stamp.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, photography by Cyril Marcilhacy.
  • Ghanaian-Scottish architect Lesley Lokko has nominated Courage Dzidula Kpodo as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.
  • In this interview he explains why despite growing global attention, his ambitions remain resolutely local.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, photography by Cyril Marcilhacy. unless stated.

Ghanaian-Scottish architect Lesley Lokko has nominated Courage Dzidula Kpodo as a key name to watch over the next two decades for Dezeen’s 20×20 project, sponsored by Kohler.

In this interview he explains why despite growing global attention, his ambitions remain resolutely local.

Having only graduated in 2025 from a master’s in architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) – for which he was awarded the Arthur Rotch Prize for highest overall mark – Kpodo is already someone Lokko believes will “help shape the next chapter of African architecture”.

Kpodo’s work, which sees him blur the roles of architect, artist and archivist, is focused on revealing what he calls the “silences” in prevailing narratives about Ghanaian architecture, and challenging the idea that Ghana’s future development must be a “linear prescription of urbanisation”.

If this sounds theoretical or speculative, Kpodo’s approach is anything but: the site of his MIT thesis was an almost five-acre stretch of farmland in Ghana to which he purchased a 99-year lease in 2022, and is right now using as a live site to consider alternative forms of development in the region.

Stating how, if nothing else, the purchase would “preserve the value of the money I had in my savings account,” Kpodo sees the site becoming an alternative institution of sorts, constructed using materials he has salvaged from vernacular buildings that would otherwise be demolished.

“The committee at MIT was a bit shocked, because they weren’t used to the idea of a thesis project existing in the real world,” Kpodo told Dezeen. “But I still thought of it as almost as a sort of sketch, just at 1:1 scale.”.

“Doing that gives you something to test – people are going to interface with it; you can test out its failures and success very quickly.”.

Growing up in Kumasi, Kpodo initially focused on visual art in school before pursuing a course in architecture at the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST), and subsequently MIT.

At KNUST he was quickly exposed to narratives around both architectural success and Ghana’s own architectural history that left him seeking something more “homegrown”.

“We had a lecture from Francis Kéré in which he spoke about his Serpentine Pavilion, and how taking on commissions from big institutions or big clients can become critical for defining your practice,” said Kpodo.

I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the big commissions to come?

“At the time, I couldn’t imagine any of these commissions coming to those of us working in the South. I couldn’t see any architects who were operating on that scale, or even at a kind of global scale,” he continued.

It has been revealed that “It almost had the opposite effect on me. I thought: okay, what can I do now that is within my means instead of waiting for the big commissions to come? I think it’s by being local that I can have something to offer to the world.”.

Kpodo became interested in local architectural archives, initially those of the KNUST Development Office, but also the less formalised collections of images and drawings that he encountered online.

He soon helped establish Postbox Ghana, a research collective initiated by artist Manuela Nebuloni to create an alternative architectural archive using postcards and stamps from the 1950s to the 1980s, which often depicted examples of Tropical Modernism and state infrastructure constructed following Ghana’s independence.

However, Kpodo still felt that these archival materials did not speak to his own understanding of Ghanaian architecture, having grown up in a “not-so-well-to-do context” in Kumasi and only really encountering modernist architecture when first entering the KNUST campus.

It has been revealed that “The whole archive that I was exposed to, whether it was in the Development Office or in the postcards, had a huge, significant gap in it,” he said. “I remember stories my dad would tell me about building practices and cultures that just didn’t make it into this archive or our training in architecture school.”.

In a recent development, “As a newly independent country, Ghana wanted to break away from any kind of ethnographic notion of what the ‘Gold Coast’ – to use its colonial name – was. So those ‘traditional’ buildings and other forms of practices did not make it into the framework of thinking about what our future meant,” he continued.

“But even though these buildings are far removed from the city centres and from the archive, they were foundational in the sense that they enabled the cocoa industry, and brought in the money that built the institutions and structures that are enshrined in postcards.”.

Kpodo began to photograph these vernacular buildings himself, many of them farm structures made using laterite, a type of local red earth that is formed into air and sun-dried blocks for construction.

Sources indicate that when I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’.

Upon finding many of these buildings slated for demolition, Kpodo has more recently begun to purchase them, before carefully deconstructing their laterite structures to become the raw material for upcoming structures on his land.

It has been revealed that the idea was initially met locally with some confusion. “I remember one man mentioned, ‘oh, are you going to extract gold from the walls?’ because laterite can contain gold,” he recalled.

Recent findings suggest that “But when I talk about rebuilding them, it usually lands. People get it, and then they begin asking, ‘okay, but what can it be?’ And then some kids would even begin making their own proposals. For me, just creating that imagination is worth it.”.

Recent findings suggest that the land that Kpodo purchased in 2022 is in Ghana’s eastern region, and was at the frontier of cocoa production in the early 1900s. Some descendants of the first farmers on the land are still based there, and were among those Kpodo interviewed to understand the history of the landscape.

Alongside the widening of a communal path – the focus of his MIT thesis – and the moving of vernacular building materials there, he has also constructed a simple timber deck, both as a rest point for the farmers and an observation point for watching future changes unfold on the site.

According to recent reports, if I were asked to design a Serpentine Pavilion, I’d probably make a replica in Ghana, too. You can only do so much in an exhibition setting.

Kpodo envisions that this future will include both new agricultural processing facilities for the farmers on the land, as well as community spaces that enable further discussions around its ongoing development.

Recent findings suggest that this work also forms the basis of Kpodo’s educational and curatorial work. He is keen to continue “speaking both languages” – the more practical with the conceptual – but he feels the latter should always be grounded in a “local base” rather than detached from it.

Industry observers note that in 2023, his work with Postbox Ghana was exhibited at both Vantage Point Sharjah and the Venice Architecture Biennale. In 2025, he curated the LagosPhoto Biennial alongside Maria Pia Bernardoni and Robin Beth Riskin, with the theme of Incarceration.

Kpodo also taught on the one-month Nomadic African Studio at the African Futures Institute, founded by Lokko as a space “dedicated to rethinking education, culture, and practice from the African continent outward.”.

Most recently, he orchestrated the transportation of the wall of a laterite farmhouse a little further afield to the Fondation Cartier in Paris, as part of the exhibition Ibrahim Mahama: Harvest Season, where it is accompanied by images from the Postbox Ghana archives.

It has been revealed that “If I were asked to design a Serpentine Pavilion, I’d probably make a replica in Ghana, too,” he stated. “You can only do so much in an exhibition setting. You can only talk so much. If the work has no ground and no local base, then I think it becomes very difficult for you to bridge what it is that you’re presenting versus the work that it proposes to be doing.”.

“We need to cultivate other sites that do the real work, sites that translate it into something which is not necessarily concerned with an educated audience,” he continued.

“My sense is that we’re increasingly going to see the most ‘powerful’ institutions seek out these hyper-local narratives and projects as a way to really understand the world.”.

Recent findings suggest that to celebrate Dezeen’s 20th birthday, we asked 20 of the most influential architects and designers of the last 20 years to identify someone they think will have a major impact in the next 20 years. Over the next four weeks, we’ll reveal their picks in a series of profile interviews.

Text description provided by the architects. The Grand Terminal provides berths for two megaships, which can enjoy a variety of leisure and cultural amenities offered by the impressive waterside complex. Hassell Principal and Head of Design Ashley Munday said, "We are really excited that our Grand Terminal is beginning its life as a festival venue for the World Cup, but what excites us even more is its future as a loved piece of the city, embedded in the cultural fabric of Doha. It is a building that doesn't just have a singular function as a cruise terminal, but has been designed to absorb other uses during the year, like markets, exhibitions, and festivals. For us, this is a civic project that has to respond to many complex needs and requirements at once, but still has an 'outward' role to face the world and welcome people into a place that is really just emerging as a destination.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Earn Alaska miles through the Alaska Airlines Visa, Marriott Bonvoy® transfers (3:1 ratio with 5K bonus per 60K), or direct purchase during sales. Target 60,000 miles for a one-way business class ticket.

Use JAL's own award search tool to check business class availability before contacting Alaska. Search 331 days out from your desired travel date. Look for flights showing "Partner Award" availability on JAL's calendar.

Industry observers note that verify your target flight operates a Boeing 787 or 777 with JAL's "Sky Suite" business class product. Older aircraft on some routes may have a less desirable cabin configuration. Check SeatGuru or JAL's fleet page.

It has been revealed that phone Alaska's award desk at 1-800-252-7522. Have your dates, route, and JAL flight number ready. The agent will search their system and process the redemption. Expect $25-$50 in taxes and fees.

Picture this: you board a Japan Airlines Boeing 787-9 at Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, turn left, and settle into your own private suite. The JAL Sky Suite III closes around you — a fully flat bed, a sliding privacy door, direct aisle access from every seat. A flight attendant in a crisp kimono-inspired uniform takes your drink order before pushback. You're cruising at 35,000 feet over the Pacific in a cabin that feels more like a boutique hotel than an airplane, and you paid for it with points you earned on everyday spending. That's the experience this redemption delivers — and the math behind it is what makes the ChooseFI community absolutely love it. A JAL Business Class ticket from Seattle (SEA) to Tokyo Narita (NRT) typically retails between **$5,000 and $10,000** in cash. That's a real number — pull up JAL.com on any given date and you'll see it. Yet Alaska Mileage Plan prices this exact award at just **60,000 miles** one way. On a $5,000 ticket, that's **8.3 cents per point**. On a $10,000 ticket — which is common during peak travel periods — that's a staggering **16.7 cents per point**. The ChooseFI benchmark for a "good" redemption is typically 1.5 to 2 cents per point. This blows past that by a factor of five to ten. Why does this gap exist? Because Alaska Mileage Plan uses a **fixed award chart** to price partner redemptions. They set the JAL Business Class rate years ago and haven't moved it in step with rising cash fares. As international business class prices have climbed, the points cost has stayed anchored — and that's the pricing inefficiency that savvy travelers exploit. This isn't a loophole that disappears tomorrow. JAL and Alaska have a deep, long-standing partnership. Alaska has consistently maintained this pricing as one of the crown jewels of its partner award chart. For anyone building toward financial independence who also wants to see the world in comfort, this redemption represents exactly what the FI travel rewards philosophy is about: using the system's own rules to access experiences that cash-wealthy people pay enormous sums for, nearly free.

A sweet spot that punches far above its weight in cents-per-mile value.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you see it, and understanding it will help you recognize similar opportunities across the loyalty landscape.

Alaska's Fixed Award Chart Is the Key.

In a recent development, most major airline programs have shifted to dynamic pricing — meaning award costs fluctuate with demand, just like cash prices. Alaska Mileage Blueprint has largely resisted this for its partner awards. JAL Business Class from North America is priced at a flat 60,000 Alaska miles one way, period. It doesn't matter if it's Golden Week in Japan or a random Tuesday in February. The chart price holds.

This creates an extraordinary opportunity because JAL cash fares are not fixed. They respond to demand, fuel costs, seasonality, and competitive dynamics. When those fares rise — as they have substantially in recent years — your 60,000 miles buy proportionally more value. The inefficiency widens the more expensive the cash fare becomes.

Here's a detail that separates Alaska from many other programs: Alaska Mileage Strategy charges zero fuel surcharges on any partner award booking. This is significant. Some programs (looking at you, British Airways Avios) pass through carrier-imposed surcharges that can add $400–$800 to a theoretically cheap award. With Alaska, your out-of-pocket is taxes only — typically $50–$150 on a transpacific itinerary. Your 60,000-mile redemption costs you 60,000 miles plus roughly $100. Full stop.

The Transfer Path: Marriott Bonvoy® Is Your On-Ramp.

Alaska Mileage Plan has no direct credit card transfer partners in the traditional Chase/Amex/Citi sense. This is the most key nuance of this redemption to understand. You cannot transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards directly to Alaska. Instead, the primary transfer path runs through Marriott Bonvoy®.

The ratio is 3 Marriott points to 1 Alaska mile, and transfers typically take 1 to 5 days to complete.
